Title and setting from the Workshop bible v1.0.1 row w02 (The Turnstile's Memory; a 24-hour swimming pool's turnstile): the catalog's lld row w02 has no setting and only the placeholder title "LRU cache". Concepts are the catalog's two w02 slugs; "o-operations" is the catalog's slug for the syllabus's "O(1) operations". The bible's three wrong options were cut to two (a faster chip; count and sort); emptying the memory every night was left out.
title: The Turnstile's Memory

post.author: u/workshop_nights_odgerel
post.title: I finish my late great-aunt's machines at night. Her turnstile program finds 99% of swimmers in its memory, and every swipe now takes 2.4 s. A swimmer timed it with her lap watch.

blocks.text: My great-aunt, Winifrith Torvaine, built coin machines and automata for sixty years. She died in the spring and left me her workshop. Each half-finished machine has a work order tied to it with string, and a program to match. I finish them at night.

This one is the turnstile at Dipperwell, a swimming pool open 24 hours. A swimmer touches a membership card to the reader, and the reader asks the pool's online system, a program on a distant computer that knows every member, whether that card may enter. Each answer takes 0.8 s: the question crosses the internet and back.
The work order: remember the last 5,000 members seen, most recent first, so most swimmers skip that wait. A store of recent answers kept close at hand is called a cache.

Winifrith had started it as a plain list: entries side by side in numbered places, like names on a register. I finished it. Each line below is one step of a swipe; the words after // say what it does:

swipe(card):
  place = entries.find(card)         // walk from the front
  if found: entries.removeAt(place)  // the rest shift up
  else:
    ask the online system            // 0.8 s
    if full: entries.removeLast()    // full = 5,000 entries
  entries.insertAtFront(card)        // all shift down

In words: first the reader walks the list from the front until it finds the card. If found, it takes that entry out, and every entry behind shifts up a place. If not, it asks the online system, and drops the last entry if the list is full. Last, it puts the card at the front, and every entry shifts down a place.
The list lives on the reader's memory chip, the small part that stores its data. Reading or moving one entry there takes 0.24 ms, thousandths of a second.
Dipperwell fitted it on Monday 14 September. The list started empty, grew with every new face, and reached 5,000 entries on Tuesday this week. The morning queue had been growing for about a week.

On Friday the 06:00 rush began at 05:55:00, a swimmer reaching the turnstile every 2 s. Mrs Wojtyna joined the queue at 05:58:00, 16th in line, and timed every swipe ahead of her on her lap watch: 2.4 s each. She got through at 05:58:39 and went straight to the front desk.

Yevdokia, the manager, emailed me her complaint and the reader's log. Each line shows a card, when its swimmer queued, when the swipe began, whether the card was found in memory, and how long it took:

At 06:00 the reader's dashboard, its status screen, showed the last 100 swipes: 99 found in memory, 99%. The one not found was a member who joined on Thursday. Before the memory, every swipe took 0.8 s and nobody queued.
Ninety-nine in a hundred found, and every swipe three times as slow as when it remembered no one.
Beside the program, Winifrith's notebook says: "Never count along the string to find a bead." I took it for a note about her automata.
Yevdokia wants it right before Monday's rush. What should I change?

comments.author: u/grey_pager
comments.text: Your dashboard counts whether a card was found. It says nothing about how long finding it took. Count the work in one found swipe: how many entries does the reader read on the way, how many shift up to close the gap, and how many shift down at the front? Does the total depend on where the card was? Programmers write a cost that grows with the length of a list as O(n), said "order n": twice the entries, twice the work. A cost that stays the same however long the list grows is O(1), "order one". Which of your steps is O(1) today? Then work out what a found swipe cost in the first week.

replies.author: u/workshop_nights_odgerel
replies.text: Found anywhere, it reads the entries up to the card, shifts the ones behind it, then shifts all of them again: 10,000 reads and moves for a list of 5,000 entries, wherever the card sat. At 0.24 ms each, that is 2.4 s. When the list held 1,000 entries, in the first week, a found swipe took 0.48 s. A card not found now takes 3.2 s. Only dropping the last entry is O(1).

comments.author: u/swap_the_chip_jarogniew
comments.text: 0.24 ms to read one entry is a museum piece. Leave the program alone: it found 99 swimmers in 100, so it works. The slow part is the chip. Fit a faster one and every walk shrinks with it. A new chip costs less than another night of your time.

replies.author: u/workshop_nights_odgerel
replies.text: The turnstile's maker sells one reader that fits the housing. Its chip is twice as fast, and Yevdokia could have it here in 10 days.

comments.author: u/short_list_pelagia
comments.text: 5,000 entries is far too many to walk. Keep the last 500 and every walk is a tenth as long. Most of your 06:00 crowd swam yesterday, so they'd still be in a short list.

replies.author: u/workshop_nights_odgerel
replies.text: Yevdokia checked the online system's records for Friday's rush. For 80 of the 100 swimmers, fewer than 500 other members had come in since their last swim.

comments.author: u/count_them_bonifacy
comments.text: Regulars belong at the front. Keep a count of each member's swipes and sort the list by count after every swipe: daily swimmers rise to the top and are found in a step or two. And stop pushing entries along the chip. Let each entry store a link to the entry before it and the entry after it, so taking one out means joining its two neighbours to each other, and nothing else moves. That's a two-way linked list.

replies.author: u/workshop_nights_odgerel
replies.text: I did think of a table that goes from a card number straight to its entry in one step, like numbered pigeonholes; programmers call it a map. But a map keeps no order. On its own it can't tell me who swam least recently, so it can't say which entry to drop.

reply.prompt: Monday's 06:00 rush comes in three days. What should Odgerel change in the turnstile's memory? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Keep a map from each card to its entry, and link entries both ways, newest first.
options.part2: I rewrote the memory on Saturday night. Each entry now holds a link to the entry before it and the entry after it, newest first, and a map goes from each card number straight to its entry. A found swipe is 6 steps: 1 look-up in the map, 2 link changes to lift the entry out, and 3 to tie it in at the front. At 0.24 ms a step that is 1.44 ms, whatever the list holds. When the list is full, the entry at the back, which the back link names, is untied and taken out of the map in 3 steps. I replayed Friday's rush through it: nobody queued, and the new member waited 0.8 s for the online system and walked on. The map and the links take more room on the chip than the plain list did; it had room to spare. I swapped the program at 03:00 on Sunday, the quietest hour, and the desk let in the one swimmer who came while the reader restarted. On Monday Mrs Wojtyna timed the turnstile again and wrote "fixed" across her complaint.
options.senior: Each of the memory's three jobs needs its own tool. The map answers "where is this card?" in one step. The two-way links keep the use order, so an entry can be lifted out and put at the front by changing a few links, and the oldest is always at the back. Together every swipe is a fixed handful of steps, O(1), so the list can hold 5,000 or 50,000 entries at the same speed. The cost is room: two links and a map slot per entry.

options.text: Fit the maker's reader, whose chip is twice as fast, so every walk takes half as long.
options.verdict: Buys one doubling, then it's back
options.part2: Yevdokia ordered the maker's reader. It came 10 days later, and until then the morning queue came back every day. The turnstile was off for a morning while the new reader went in; the desk let swimmers in by hand against a printed list of cards. A found swipe then took 1.2 s, and Friday's rush, replayed, had no queue. But 1.2 s is still slower than the 0.8 s the old reader took with no memory at all, and the cost still grows with the list. In January the New Year offer brought new members, Yevdokia asked for 10,000 entries, and once the list filled a found swipe took 2.4 s again. With a rush like Friday's, 16 people were queueing at 05:58:00, and the last waited 40.4 s.
options.senior: A faster chip divides the cost by a fixed amount; it doesn't change how the cost grows. The plain list is still O(n): every found swipe touches every entry twice, so twice the entries undoes twice the speed. Hardware is the right answer when the work is already as small as it can be. Here the work was 10,000 steps where about 6 would do.

options.text: Keep only the last 500 entries, so every walk and shift is a tenth as long as now.
options.part2: I cut the memory to 500 entries on Saturday night. A found swipe now reads and moves 1,000 entries: 0.24 s. I replayed Friday's rush through it: 80 of the 100 swimmers were found and 20 were not, and each of those 20 waited for the online system, 1.04 s in all. Nobody queued. But the dashboard now reads 80%, and the online system now answers about 20 swipes in every 100 where it used to answer 1. When it is slow, or down, one swimmer in five feels it at the turnstile, and the desk lets them in by hand. And the list is still walked end to end: if the pool ever needs a longer memory, the queue comes back with it.
options.senior: A shorter list makes each O(n) swipe cheaper by making n small, and it works: no queue. But it pays in forgetting. The cache now drops anyone who hasn't swum in about a day, so 1 swipe in 5 goes back to the slow online system, and the turnstile depends on that system far more than before. It is a fair stopgap for Monday; it is not the design, because the cost still grows with the size you need.

options.text: Count each member's swipes, and sort the list by count after every swipe, top first.
options.part2: I added a count to every entry and a sort after each swipe. The sort reads all 5,000 entries and writes them back in order, so a swipe took at least 2.4 s, no faster than before. I replayed Friday's rush through it: 16 people were still queueing at 05:58:00. Worse, the order went wrong. Members who swam daily in September kept their high counts and sat at the front for good, though some had stopped coming. New members started with a count of 1, so they sat at the back and were the first dropped when the list was full: the member who joined on Thursday was sent to the online system on her next visits too.
options.senior: Sorting on every swipe adds work that touches every entry, so it can't be faster than the walk it replaces. And counting all-time swipes answers a different question, "who swam most, ever", not "who swam last". Old counts never fade and new members never get a foothold; Redis's frequency-based mode, for one, uses "a decay period so that the counter is reduced over time". The fix for a slow cache is a better structure, not a different order on the same slow one.

sim.title: Replay Friday's rush through the turnstile
sim.lede: You're Odgerel, replaying Friday's 06:00 rush at Dipperwell from 05:55:00, before the first swipe. 100 swimmers reach the turnstile, one every 2 s, and it handles one swipe at a time; the rest queue. Each swimmer's place in the list comes from the online system's records: 80 sit in the first 500 places, 82 in the first 1,000, 87 in the first 2,000 and 99 in the first 5,000. Swimmer 40 joined on Thursday and is in no list. A plain list costs 2 steps for every entry it holds, found or not: the walk and the shifts. Each step takes 0.24 ms on the chip, or 0.12 ms on the faster chip. A card not found also waits 0.8 s for the online system. The list is full at every size you pick. The sim counts the sort as reading and writing every entry, and leaves out its walk, so its times are the least it could take. The map with links takes 6 steps for a found card and 8 for a new one. Pick a design and how many entries the memory keeps.
sim.tryThis: Try this: press Step once, then Play the rush, and read the queue at 05:58:00 and the longest wait. Switch to no memory: 0.8 s a swipe and no queue. Back on the plain list, set 1,000 entries and read a found swipe's time. Try the faster chip at 5,000 entries, then at 10,000. Try 500 entries and read the found count. Last, the map with links, at 5,000 entries and at 10,000.

explain.oneLine: The memory found almost everyone; finding them was the slow part. A plain list makes every found swipe read and move 10,000 entries at 0.24 ms each, 2.4 s, so swimmers arriving every 2 s queued.

steps.title: Found, and still slow.
steps.text: A cache is worth having only if a found answer is quicker than asking. The dashboard counted found swipes, 99 in 100, and said nothing about what each one cost. Follow one found swipe through the plain list. First the reader walks from the front until it reaches the card, reading each entry on the way. Then it takes the entry out, and every entry behind it shifts up a place. Then it puts the card at the front, and every entry shifts down a place. However far down the card was, the reads and the first shifts add up to the whole list, and the second shifts are the whole list again: 2 × 5,000 = 10,000 steps, at 0.24 ms each, 2.4 s. A card not found walks the whole list, waits 0.8 s, and shifts the whole list: 3.2 s. The old reader, with no memory, took 0.8 s for everyone.

steps.title: O(n): the cost grows with the list.
steps.text: When a step's cost grows in step with the number of entries, n, it is O(n), said "order n". The plain list's swipe is O(n): at 1,000 entries a found swipe took 0.48 s, at 5,000 it took 2.4 s, and at 10,000 it would take 4.8 s. That is why nothing went wrong on the first day and everything went wrong a month later: the list filled one new face at a time, and the swipe slowed with it. A step whose cost stays the same at any size is O(1), "order one". In the plain list only dropping the last entry was O(1). A faster chip divides an O(n) cost by a fixed amount; doubling the list wins it back.

steps.title: Why 0.4 s became a 40 s wait.
steps.text: In the rush a swimmer reached the turnstile every 2 s, and each swipe took 2.4 s. A turnstile that is slower than its arrivals never catches up: each swimmer waited 0.4 s longer than the one before. By 05:58:00, 75 swipes had begun and 91 swimmers had arrived, so 16 stood in the queue. The 100th swimmer, at 05:58:18, waited 40.4 s. Below 2 s a swipe, the same rush leaves no queue at all: that is why the old reader's 0.8 s was fine, and why a small slowdown per swipe turned into a long line all at once.

steps.title: The fix: a map to each entry, and links both ways.
steps.text: Give each job its own tool. Keep the entries in a two-way linked list, newest at the front and oldest at the back: each entry holds a link to the one before and the one after. Keep a map from card number to that card's entry. For a found card, first the map gives its entry in 1 step; if the map and the list ever disagree, it can point at an entry no longer there, so both must change together. Second, its two neighbours are linked to each other in 2 steps, which lifts it out; nothing else moves, but if one of the two links is skipped, the list keeps a path to an entry that has left it. Third, it is tied in at the front in 3 steps: its two links and the old front's back link; miss the last one and the list can no longer be walked back from the front. For a new card when the list is full, the back entry, which the back link names, is untied and removed from the map, and the new card goes in at the front and into the map. Every swipe is 6 or 8 steps, O(1), at 5,000 entries or 50,000. Winifrith's line was this design: a bead on a string should never be found by counting along the string.

diagram.aria: The fix, drawn just before card 46203 swipes. A row of entries linked both ways, newest on the left: card 10527, newest; 409 more entries, 2nd to 410th; card 46203, 411th; 4,588 more entries; and the oldest entry, 5,000th, at the right. A map above points straight to card 46203 in 1 step. A note says moving it to the front takes 5 link changes and nothing else moves.

notes.text: to the front: 5 link changes, nothing else moves

explain.caption: The fix, drawn just before card 46203 swipes. The map jumps straight to its entry, 411th in line, in 1 step. Its two neighbours are joined to each other, and it is tied in at the front: 5 link changes, and none of the other 4,999 entries moves. The oldest entry is always the one at the back, so a full list knows what to drop without looking.

fix.title: The fix: a map to every entry, and the entries linked both ways
fix.text: Keep the 5,000 entries as a two-way linked list in use order, newest at the front, oldest at the back, and keep a map from each card number to its entry. On a found card: look it up in the map, join its two neighbours to each other, and tie it in at the front, 6 steps in all. On a new card: ask the online system; if the list is full, untie the back entry and remove it from the map; then tie the new card in at the front and add it to the map, 8 steps plus the 0.8 s wait. Change the map and the links together, every time, so they never disagree. Before writing your own, check whether your language already has one: Java's LinkedHashMap in access order, or Python's lru_cache, are this design.

limits: Every entry now carries two links and a map slot as well as its card number, so the same 5,000 members take more room on the chip. On a reader with no room to spare, the same design would hold fewer members.
The memory says only that a card was allowed in when it was last asked about. While a card keeps being found, the reader never asks the online system about it again.

A map finds an entry in 1 step on average; many card numbers landing in the same slot slow it down. And if two parts of a program ever swipe at once, the map and the links must change together under one lock.

explain.seniorTake: A cache has two numbers, and dashboards usually show only one. How often it finds the answer is the hit rate; what a hit costs is the other, and a cache whose hits cost more than asking is worse than none. When you build one, write down each job it does, find, move to the front, drop the oldest, and the cost of each as the cache grows. Any job that walks the entries is O(n), and it will feel fine until the day the cache is full. The map plus two-way linked list makes every job O(1) and is common enough that many languages ship it, so reach for the library first. Then measure both numbers, and size the cache for the hit rate you need, knowing the cost per hit no longer depends on that size.

realWorld.title: Python's lru_cache counts hits, not time
realWorld.text: The Python docs describe functools.lru_cache as a "Decorator to wrap a function with a memoizing callable that saves up to the maxsize most recent calls." To tune it, it offers "a cache_info() function that returns a named tuple showing hits, misses, maxsize and currsize". Like Dipperwell's dashboard, it counts hits and misses; how long each took is yours to measure.

realWorld.title: Inside lru_cache: a dictionary and a circular two-way list
realWorld.text: CPython's own source for lru_cache builds the fix described here. It sets "cache = {}" for the look-up, comments "# Size limited caching that tracks accesses by recency", and marks its list's starting point "# root of the circular doubly linked list". On a hit: "# Move the link to the front of the circular queue".

realWorld.title: Java's LinkedHashMap: the same shape, in the standard library
realWorld.text: Java's documentation says LinkedHashMap "maintains a doubly-linked list running through all of its entries", can keep them in "access-order", and that "This kind of map is well-suited to building LRU caches." removeEldestEntry "may be overridden to impose a policy for removing stale mappings automatically when new mappings are added to the map." It gives "constant-time performance for the basic operations (add, contains and remove), assuming the hash function disperses elements properly among the buckets."

realWorld.title: Redis trades exact order for memory
realWorld.text: Recalling s2e10: the Redis docs say its LRU "uses an approximation of the least recently used keys rather than calculating them exactly. It samples a small number of keys at random and then evicts the ones with the longest time since last access." And why: "The reason Redis does not use a true LRU implementation is because it costs more memory." The links that make each swipe O(1) are exactly that memory.

realWorld.title: Why a plain list shifts
realWorld.text: The Python wiki's time-complexity page says "Internally, a list is represented as an array", and that the largest costs come from "inserting or deleting somewhere near the beginning (because everything after that must move)." Its tables list a list's Insert and Delete Item as O(n) on average, and a dict's Get Item, Set Item and Delete Item as O(1) on average.

asked: Design an LRU cache with O(1) get and put.
Why a doubly linked list, and not a singly linked one?
Is a hash map really O(1)?
interview.answer: Keep two structures that always change together. A hash map from key to node gives any entry in one step. A doubly linked list holds the nodes in use order, most recent at the head, least recent at the tail; dummy head and tail nodes save edge cases. get(key): look the node up in the map; if it's missing, it's a miss; if found, unlink it by joining its prev and next, and insert it after the head, then return its value. put(key, value): if the key exists, update the value and move it to the head; if not, create a node at the head and add it to the map, and if the size is now over capacity, unlink the tail's node and delete its key from the map, which is why each node stores its key. Every step is a fixed number of pointer changes, so both operations are O(1). It must be doubly linked because removing a node needs its predecessor, and a singly linked list can only find that by walking from the head, which is O(n). A hash map is O(1) on average, assuming the hash spreads keys well; with many collisions it degrades toward O(n). In practice, use the library: Java's LinkedHashMap in access order with removeEldestEntry, or Python's functools.lru_cache for a function's results. Then say the trade-offs: two pointers and a map entry per item, a lock or a thread-safe version if threads share it, and why systems like Redis approximate LRU to save that memory. Finally, measure both the hit rate and the cost per hit.

terms.def: Odgerel's great-aunt, who built coin machines and automata for sixty years and, late in life, small programs for local businesses. Her workshop is full of unfinished machines.
The paper tied to each unfinished machine in the workshop, saying what the client asked for. The turnstile's asked the reader to remember the last 5,000 members.
A machine that moves by itself, such as a clockwork figure that writes or plays. Winifrith built them alongside coin machines.
The swimming pool in this story, open 24 hours a day. Yevdokia manages it; its 06:00 rush is the busiest moment at the turnstile.
A gate with turning arms that lets one person through at a time once the card reader says yes. Like a ticket barrier at a station.
The box by the turnstile that a member touches their card to. It holds the memory and asks the online system about cards it doesn't know.
The pool's program on a distant computer that knows every member and says whether a card may enter. Each answer takes 0.8 s, because the question crosses the internet and back.
A store of recent answers kept close at hand, so you don't have to ask the slow source again (s2e04). The turnstile's memory of its last 5,000 members is one.
A hit is an answer found in the cache; a miss is one that isn't, so the slow source must be asked (s2e04). The dashboard's "found in memory" counts hits.
The share of look-ups the cache answers itself: 99 of 100 swipes is 99%. It says nothing about how long each hit took.
One member's place in the memory: their card number, and that the card may enter.
Entries stored side by side in numbered places, like names on a register. Taking one out or putting one at the front means moving every entry after it.
Read entries one after another from the front until the one you want turns up. The further down it is, the more entries you read.
Move every entry along by one place to close a gap or make room. On the turnstile's chip each entry moved takes 0.24 ms.
The small part of the card reader that stores its data. Reading or moving one entry on it takes 0.24 ms.
Short for millisecond, a thousandth of a second. 0.24 ms is about a four-thousandth of a second.
Reading, moving or changing one entry, link or map slot on the chip: 0.24 ms each, or 0.12 ms on the faster chip.
The reader's status screen. It showed the last 100 swipes and how many were found in memory.
A line where each person waits their turn. At the turnstile it forms whenever a swipe takes longer than the gap between swimmers.
A swimmer's stopwatch for timing lengths. Mrs Wojtyna used hers to time each swipe at 2.4 s.
Said "order n": a cost that grows in step with the number of entries, n. Twice the entries, twice the work. The plain list's swipe is O(n).
Said "order one": a cost that stays the same however many entries there are. Each step of the fixed memory is O(1).
The O( ) way of writing how a cost grows as the data grows, ignoring fixed amounts. O(1) stays flat; O(n) grows in step with n.
Another name for O(1): the same number of steps at any size.
A table that goes from a key, such as a card number, straight to its entry in one step on average, like numbered pigeonholes. It keeps no order of its own.
The rule a map uses to turn a key into a slot number. If it sends many keys to the same slot, look-ups slow down.
Entries that each hold a link to the entry before and the entry after. One can be lifted out by joining its two neighbours, without moving any others.
A stored note of where another entry is, so the program can go straight to it.
Put entries in order by some value, such as a count of swipes. A sort has to look at every entry at least once.
A rule for a full cache: drop the entry used longest ago (s2e04). The turnstile's memory is an LRU cache.
A rule for a full cache: drop the entry used fewest times (s2e04). Counting swipes and dropping the lowest count is one; real ones let old counts fade.
Drop an entry from a full cache to make room for a new one (s2e04).
LRU that samples a few entries and drops the least recently used of those, rather than keeping exact order. Redis does this to save memory (s2e10).
A popular program that keeps data in memory, often used as a cache (s2e04, s2e10).
A programming language. Its standard library includes functools.lru_cache, an LRU cache for a function's results.
A programming language. Its standard library includes LinkedHashMap, a map with a two-way linked list through its entries.
Python's ready-made LRU cache: wrap a function in it, and it remembers the results of its most recent calls, up to maxsize.
A wrapper put around a function to add a duty, such as remembering its results, without changing the function's own code.
Remembering a function's answer for the inputs it was given, so the same question isn't worked out twice.
In lru_cache, the most results it will keep, and how many it holds now.
In Python, a small fixed bundle of values with a name for each, such as hits and misses.
Python's built-in map: a key goes straight to its value. lru_cache uses one for its look-up.
The main program that runs Python code. Its source code is public, including lru_cache's.
A two-way linked list whose last entry links back to the first, joined through one fixed starting entry (the root). lru_cache keeps its use order this way.
Java's map with a two-way linked list running through its entries. In access order it keeps them from least to most recently used.
Keeping entries in the order they were last used, rather than the order they were added.
A LinkedHashMap method you can override to drop the oldest entry whenever a new one is added: how it becomes an LRU cache.
One slot in a hash map. Keys that land in the same bucket have to be told apart one by one.
A rule that lets only one part of a program change something at a time (s5e01). The map and the links must change together under one.
How long a cached answer may be used before it must be asked for again (s2e04).
Removing or marking a cached answer as out of date because the source has changed (s2e04).
The maker's replacement reader: the same plain list, at 0.12 ms a step instead of 0.24 ms.
How many members the memory holds: 500, 1,000, 2,000, 5,000 or 10,000. The story's is 5,000.
Information about an identifiable living person. A card number tied to when its member swims is personal data.
The article of the EU's data protection law that sets the principles for personal data, among them data minimisation (1)(c) and storage limitation (1)(e).
Keeping only the personal data a purpose needs. The turnstile's memory needs a card number and a yes, not names or addresses.
Keeping personal data in a form that identifies people no longer than the purpose needs.

atWork: Look for caches in your own code that are built on a plain list or array: a search through the entries, then a remove and an insert at the front. They are easy to write, they pass every test with a few hundred entries, and they slow down a little with every entry until the day they are full. Read-only access to the code is enough to find them. Then measure two numbers, not one: the hit rate, and the time a hit takes at the cache's full size. Prefer the library structure, Java's LinkedHashMap in access order or Python's functools.lru_cache, over a hand-written one. If the cache holds personal data, such as member or customer ids, and you handle EU residents' data, GDPR Art. 5(1)(c) asks that data be "adequate, relevant and limited to what is necessary in relation to the purposes for which they are processed": keep the id and the answer, not names or addresses. Art. 5(1)(e) asks that it be "kept in a form which permits identification of data subjects for no longer than is necessary", so set a size limit or an expiry on every cache of people's data from the first draft, rather than adding one at audit time.

recall.prompt: Your team's web shop keeps its last 10,000 product pages in memory as a plain array, newest first. On each request it searches the array, takes the page out and puts it back at the front. It finds 97% of requests, yet pages got slower each week as it filled. What is going on, and how would you build it instead?

keyIdeas.idea: Every request reads and moves entries across the whole array, so a found page costs time that grows with the cache's size: O(n)
A hash map from key to entry plus a doubly linked list in use order makes find, move and drop O(1)
Prefer the library structure that already does this: LinkedHashMap in access order, or Python's lru_cache

recall.model: Finding 97% of requests says nothing about what each find costs. Every request searches the array from the front, then removing the page shifts every entry after it, and putting it at the front shifts every entry again, so even a hit touches the whole array: O(n), a cost that grows with the cache's size. It was fast when the cache was small and slowed each week as it filled. Build it as a hash map from page key to a node, plus a doubly linked list of nodes in use order: the map finds the node in one step, two link changes lift it out, a few more put it at the head, and a full cache drops the tail node and deletes its key from the map. Every operation is O(1), at any size. Better still, use the library structure that already does this, such as Java's LinkedHashMap in access order with removeEldestEntry, or Python's lru_cache where the cache is a function's results.

recall.prompt: A plain list of n entries, newest first. Each found swipe walks to the card, takes it out, and puts it at the front. The list grows from 5,000 entries to 10,000. What happens to the time of a found swipe?
options: It stays about the same, because the card was found
It roughly doubles, because the shifts cover the whole list
It roughly quadruples, because the walk and the shifts multiply
It depends only on how far down the card was
recall.why: The walk to the card plus the entries behind it shifting up add up to the whole list, and putting the card at the front shifts the whole list again: 2n steps wherever the card sat. At 0.24 ms a step, 5,000 entries cost 2.4 s and 10,000 cost 4.8 s. The steps add up; they don't multiply.

recall.prompt: The fixed turnstile memory holds 5,000 entries. Walk through one swipe for a card it already holds, and one for a brand-new card when the memory is full. Say what each part of the swipe changes, and why the number of steps doesn't depend on the 5,000.

keyIdeas.idea: The map gives the card's entry in one step, with no walk
The entry is lifted out by joining its two neighbours, and tied in at the front; nothing else moves
When full, the back entry is untied and removed from the map too, then the new card goes in at the front and into the map

recall.model: For a card it holds: the map goes straight to that card's entry in one step. The entry's two neighbours are joined to each other, which lifts it out; then it is tied in at the front, changing its own two links and the old front's back link. Nothing else moves: 6 steps. For a new card when the memory is full: the map has no entry, so the reader asks the online system. The back entry, the least recently used, is untied from its neighbour and removed from the map too, and the new card is tied in at the front and added to the map: 8 steps plus the wait. No step reads entries one after another, so the count is the same at 5,000 entries or 50,000.

recall.prompt: Why does Redis approximate LRU, sampling a few keys and evicting the least recently used of those, instead of keeping every key in exact use order?
options: Exact use order would drop the wrong keys more often
Redis can only sort keys by name, not by use
Keeping exact use order costs more memory
Exact use order only works with a single client
recall.why: The Redis docs: "The reason Redis does not use a true LRU implementation is because it costs more memory." Exact order needs links on every key, the room the turnstile's fix pays for its 5,000 entries. Redis samples instead, and says "the approximation is virtually equivalent for an application using Redis."

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 3 months later. The map and the links have kept the 06:00 rush moving since October; nobody queues. But on Tuesday 12 January the desk found that a member whose membership ended on Thursday 31 December had swum every morning since. The turnstile let her in 12 times. Each time the desk asked the online system, it said no; the turnstile never asked.
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. Why did the turnstile keep letting her in, and what should the memory do so that an ended membership stops at the turnstile?

keyIdeas.idea: She was found every day, so LRU kept her entry near the front and never dropped it, and a found card is never checked with the online system again
Give each entry a time limit or keep the membership's end date in it, and ask the online system again once it passes
Or have the online system tell the reader when a membership ends, so it removes that entry

coldCase.model: LRU only drops what nobody uses. She swam every morning, so each swipe found her and moved her entry to the front, and an entry near the front is never dropped. A found card is never checked with the online system again, so the memory still held the yes it got in December. Two changes, ideally both. Give each entry a time to live, or store the membership's end date in it: after 24 hours, or once the end date passes, the reader treats the card as not found and asks the online system, which says no. And have the online system tell the reader when a membership ends, so the reader removes the entry at once; that invalidation closes the gap to minutes, and the time limit catches any message that gets lost.
